title: Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2010
portfolio: Climate Change, Energy Efficiency and Water

divisions.question: That the amendment ( **Senator Milne’s** ) be agreed to.

Consideration resumed from 22 June. Scott Ludlam We are dealing with Greens amendments (4), (9) and (1) on sheet 6114. Christine Milne I rise to respond to Senator Colbeck’s analysis of these amendments to the [Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2010](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/R4356) and related bills. These amendments are to remove any view that native forest biomass can be used to generate renewable energy certificates. Yesterday Senator Colbeck mentioned that WWF Australia supported biomass energy. The report on Forestry Tasmania’s website is a WWF report, but it refers to biomass in Europe not biomass in Australia and so WWF have put out a clarifying statement which says: ‘No support for biomass burning of native forests’. Let us make it very clear that the European situation is quite different from the situation here in Australia and WWF do not support burning of native forests for biomass in Australia. Senator Colbeck really let the cat out of the bag yesterday when he talked about the extent to which the Tasmanian logging industry is depending on getting renewable energy certificates as a lifeline for logging native forests. He said here that he would expect they would get something like 3,000 gigawatt hours, but in Forestry Tasmania’s own so-called fact sheet it says that it wants to build a 25-megawatt biomass plant at Southwood and that would generate 160,000 renewable energy certificates a year. So there is a full expectation that they would be getting RECs from their 25-megawatt biomass plant at Southwood. We have this ludicrous situation where we are logging native forests without the emissions from those native forests being counted because the Kyoto accounting does not require it. So they log the carbon stores, the most important carbon stores. If the government really wanted to move on climate change then it would protect the carbon stores and it would support this amendmen

Alan Ferguson I now put opposition amendments (1) and (2) on sheet 6158. The question is that those amendments be agreed to. Christine Milne On a point of order, Mr Chair, I just seek clarification: is this Senator Colbeck’s amendment? Alan Ferguson I am told yes. Christine Milne I have a concern because we had an arrangement with Senator Xenophon that—sorry? Alan Ferguson Senator Milne, I intend to make it another four-minute division if that may help you. Christine Milne Okay. Question put.
That the amendment ( **Senator Birmingham’s** ) be agreed to.
That the amendment ( **Senator Xenophon’s** ) be agreed to.
That the amendments ( **Senator Birmingham’s** ) be agreed to.

speeches.speaker: Ursula Stephens
speeches.brief: The bills were introduced together, and a motion was moved and agreed to for them to proceed without formalities, be taken together, and be read a first time.

speeches.speaker: Ursula Stephens
speeches.brief: The speaker tabled and moved second reading for three bills: the Airports (On-Airport Activities Administration) Validation Bill 2010 to validate potentially invalid parking infringement notices issued at 21 Commonwealth leased airports since 2004; the Australian Wine and Brandy Corporation Amendment Bill 2009 to implement the Australia-European Community Agreement on Trade in Wine, strengthen the Label Integrity Program, and update compliance provisions; and the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Digital Television) Bill 2010 to create a new satellite service delivering digital television to all Australians in black-spot areas, with three new commercial satellite licence areas (Northern Australia, South Eastern Australia, and Western Australia).

speeches.speaker: Simon Birmingham
speeches.brief: The coalition argued that the bills were necessary to fix the government's flawed renewable energy target, which caused a collapse in certificate prices and stalled large‑scale investment, and supported splitting the target into 41,000 gigawatt‑hours for large‑scale projects and an uncapped small‑scale scheme, but raised concerns about unlimited liability for electricity users, the inclusion of waste coalmine gas, and risks of another boom‑bust cycle similar to the Home Insulation Program.

speeches.speaker: Scott Ludlam
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that Greens amendments to exclude native forest biomass from renewable energy certificates should be passed, stating that logging native forests for biomass destroys carbon stores, is not renewable, and would provide a government subsidy—with an estimated 160,000 certificates per year from a proposed 25 MW plant at Southwood and 50% of revenue for the Eden mill depending on RECs.

speeches.speaker: Julian McGauran
speeches.brief: The speaker moved amendments to increase the eligible small generation unit size from 1.5kW to 3kW and to establish a mandatory inspection scheme for new installations, arguing these would provide flexibility and quality control. The government and opposition supported these amendments, which were passed.
